title: Universal Gravitation
learning_goal: Use Newton's law of universal gravitation and scientific notation to analyze gravitational force and predict how mass and distance affect gravitational interactions.

stages.title: 1. Gravity is a universal force
stages.content: Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass. The gravitational force becomes stronger when either mass increases and weaker when the distance between the objects increases.

stages.title: 2. Newton's law of universal gravitation
stages.content: The gravitational force is F = Gm₁m₂/r², where G is the universal gravitational constant, m₁ and m₂ are the two masses, and r is the center-to-center distance between them.

stages.title: 3. Worked example
stages.content: If the distance between two objects doubles while their masses stay the same, the gravitational force becomes one-fourth as large because the distance is squared in the denominator: 1/(2²) = 1/4.

stages.title: 4. Scientific notation
stages.content: Gravitational calculations often involve very large or very small numbers. Keep coefficients and powers of ten organized separately, then combine them carefully.

stages.title: 5. Guided practice
stages.prompt: Two objects have the same masses as before, but the distance between them becomes three times larger. What happens to the gravitational force?
stages.hint: The distance is squared in the denominator. Compare 1/r² with 1/(3r)².
stages.alternate_explanation: Imagine spreading the same gravitational interaction over a distance three times larger. Because distance is squared, the force falls by a factor of 3².

stages.title: 6. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, identify the variables in F = Gm₁m₂/r², predict how force changes when mass or distance changes, use scientific notation accurately, and explain gravitational effects on orbital motion.

concept_cards.title: Universal attraction
concept_cards.content: Every pair of masses attracts. Newton’s law gives F = Gm₁m₂/r², with G approximately 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². Use kilograms and meters to obtain newtons. Force acts along the line joining the masses.

concept_cards.title: Distance means center-to-center separation
concept_cards.content: For point masses, r is their separation. For nonoverlapping spherically symmetric bodies, external gravitational interactions can be calculated using their centers. Do not substitute only the surface gap.

concept_cards.title: Inverse-square reasoning
concept_cards.content: At fixed masses, tripling r reduces force to one ninth. Halving r increases force fourfold. More generally, F_new/F_old = (m₁_new/m₁_old)(m₂_new/m₂_old)/(r_new/r_old)².

concept_cards.title: Orbits are free fall
concept_cards.content: In a circular orbit, gravity provides the net inward force while velocity is tangent to the orbit. A satellite keeps missing the surface as it falls. Gravity is not zero in orbit.

concept_cards.title: Organize scientific notation
concept_cards.content: Multiply coefficients and add powers when multiplying. Divide coefficients and subtract powers when dividing. Square both the coefficient and the power of ten in r². Normalize the final coefficient to at least 1 and less than 10.

conceptual_questions.prompt: Explain why doubling the distance reduces gravity by a factor of four rather than two.
expected_ideas: Force is inversely proportional to squared separation.
Doubling separation multiplies the denominator by four.
misconceptions: The inverse-square law is an inverse linear law.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: What happens to r² when r becomes 2r?

conceptual_questions.prompt: Why does a satellite remain in orbit instead of requiring gravity to disappear?
expected_ideas: Its tangential velocity and falling motion combine into an orbit under suitable conditions.
misconceptions: Satellites orbit because there is no gravity.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: What changes the direction of its velocity?
